title: How Bookmakers Make Money
subtitle: The overround, explained with real numbers — why odds never quite add up to 100%, and what that margin actually costs you per bet.
intro: Every bookmaker's odds carry a built-in margin called the overround (or vig). It's not a conspiracy — it's simple arithmetic: price a market so the implied probabilities add up to slightly more than 100%, and the house keeps the difference regardless of the result.

On an exchange like Cricbet99, the mechanic is different. You're trading against other bettors, not against the house, so the margin comes from a small commission on net winnings rather than skewed odds — which is why exchange prices are usually sharper than a traditional bookmaker's.

This guide breaks down the maths in plain terms: how to spot the overround in any odds you're quoted, why two-way markets carry a smaller margin than three-way ones, and how commission-based exchange pricing compares in practice.

faqs.q: What is the overround in betting?
faqs.a: It's the amount by which a market's implied probabilities exceed 100%. That excess is the bookmaker's built-in edge, collected regardless of which outcome wins.

faqs.q: Do exchanges like Cricbet99 have the same margin?
faqs.a: Not quite. An exchange takes a commission on net winnings rather than pricing a margin into every outcome, which is why exchange odds are often closer to the true probability than a fixed-odds book's.

faqs.q: How can I estimate the margin on a market myself?
faqs.a: Convert each outcome's odds to an implied probability (1 ÷ decimal odds), add them together, and anything over 100% is the margin. A tighter market sits closer to 100%; a wider one sits further above it.

faqs.q: Does knowing the margin change how I should bet?
faqs.a: It won't guarantee a win, but it helps you compare markets — a tighter-margin market gives you better long-run value for the same stake.
